title: IPO
description: Brute force to optimized: recursively exploring every project sequence versus a two-heap greedy (sorted eligibility, max-heap for best profit).

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: You have w capital and can select at most k distinct projects to maximize your final capital. Project i requires at least capital[i] to start and yields profits[i] upon completion (added to your capital). Return the maximum final capital after choosing at most k projects.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","k (max projects), w (starting capital), profits, capital (per project requirements)"],["Output","Maximum final capital after selecting at most k projects"],["Goal","Greedily pick the most profitable AFFORDABLE project each round, using two heaps"],["Constraints","1 <= k <= 10^5, 0 <= w <= 10^9"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"At each step, choose the best AFFORDABLE option, capital grows over time\"","A greedy two-heap approach: a min-heap for capital requirements, a max-heap for profit among currently affordable projects"],["\"Repeat k times, choosing optimally each round\"","Greedily taking the most profitable currently-affordable project is optimal at every step"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

At each of the k rounds, the best choice is always the highest-profit project that is currently affordable (its required capital is at or below current capital). As capital grows from completed projects, more projects may become affordable, so the set of "currently affordable" projects needs to be efficiently maintained and queried for its maximum profit at every round.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reinvesting Profits into the Best Available Business Venture
blocks.text: Picture having a limited amount of startup capital and the opportunity to invest in up to k business ventures, each requiring a minimum capital to enter and yielding a specific profit. At each opportunity, the SMARTEST move is always to enter whichever affordable venture offers the highest profit, since that maximizes capital for future rounds too.

blocks.caption: A min-heap tracks capital requirements to find newly affordable projects; a max-heap tracks profit to pick the best one each round

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: k = 2, w = 0, profits = [1, 2, 3], capital = [0, 1, 1]

Result: 4. Start with w=0: only project 0 (capital 0) is affordable, take it (+1 profit, capital=1). Now projects 1 and 2 are affordable (capital 1); take project 2 (+3 profit, capital=4). Total after 2 picks: 4.
5. How Should We Think?

Before trying every possible sequence of project choices, notice that at each round, greedily choosing the highest-profit AFFORDABLE project is always optimal, since profit only ever helps future rounds too, and there is no reason to ever pick a lower-profit affordable project when a higher-profit one is available.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: At any point, only projects whose required capital is at or below the current capital are eligible; among these, picking the highest-profit one is always at least as good as any other choice, since capital only grows from taking projects (never shrinks), so a higher profit now can only help, never hurt, future eligibility.

Observation 2: Sorting all projects by required capital lets a pointer sweep through them, "unlocking" (making eligible) projects one at a time as capital grows.

Observation 3: Maintaining all currently-unlocked-but-not-yet-taken projects in a max-heap keyed by profit lets the best available choice be found in O(log n) at each round.

Observation 4: Repeating "unlock all newly affordable projects, take the best available one" exactly k times (or until no projects remain affordable) gives the maximum final capital.
This leads to sorting projects by required capital, then k rounds: unlock all newly affordable projects into a max-heap by profit, take the top (highest profit) one, and add its profit to capital.
6. Brute Force Solution
Recursively try every possible sequence of up to k distinct project choices, tracking the maximum final capital achieved across all valid sequences.
Step by step algorithm

items: At each of up to k rounds, try every currently-affordable, not-yet-used project as the next pick.
Recursively explore the resulting capital after taking each choice.
Track the maximum final capital across all explored sequences.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every possible sequence of picks directly explores every strategy, guaranteed correct.
This costs exponential time (roughly n choices at each of k rounds), infeasible beyond tiny inputs.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential, O(n^k) roughly.
Space: O(k) recursion depth plus O(n) for tracking used projects.

Limitation: since always taking the highest-profit affordable project is provably optimal (an exchange argument: swapping in a higher-profit affordable choice never hurts), a two-heap greedy approach achieves O(n log n + k log n) instead of exponential exploration.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why exploring every sequence is unnecessary: an exchange argument shows that if a suboptimal (lower-profit) affordable project is chosen when a higher-profit one was available, swapping them (or reordering to take the higher-profit one first) never decreases, and can only increase, final capital.

The two-heap greedy structure: sort projects by required capital once; maintain a pointer into this sorted list, and a max-heap (by profit) of all projects "unlocked" (capital requirement met) but not yet taken.

Each round: advance the pointer to unlock all newly affordable projects into the max-heap; pop the highest-profit one (if any) and add its profit to capital; repeat for k rounds or until the heap is empty.

The core idea: sort once, then greedily take the best currently-affordable project each round, using a max-heap for O(log n) selection.

Sort projects by required capital. For each of k rounds: unlock all newly affordable projects (capital <= current w) into a max-heap by profit; if the heap is empty, stop; otherwise pop the highest-profit project and add its profit to w.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for k=2, w=0, profits=[1, 2, 3], capital=[0, 1, 1]

blocks.caption: Sort by capital requirement once; each round, unlock new projects and take the highest-profit affordable one

codes.python:
import heapq

def find_maximized_capital(k, w, profits, capital):
    projects = sorted(zip(capital, profits))               # sort by required capital
    max_heap = []                                            # max-heap by profit (negated for min-heap)
    idx = 0
    n = len(projects)
    for _ in range(k):
        while idx < n and projects[idx][0] <= w:              # unlock newly affordable projects
            heapq.heappush(max_heap, -projects[idx][1])
            idx += 1
        if not max_heap:
            break
        w += -heapq.heappop(max_heap)                          # take the highest-profit affordable project
    return w

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since capital only ever grows from completing projects (never shrinks), any project affordable now remains affordable later, so there is no downside to delaying a lower-profit project in favor of a higher-profit one available NOW; taking the highest-profit affordable project at each round is therefore always at least as good as any other valid choice at that point, an exchange argument confirming the greedy strategy's optimality. Sorting once and unlocking newly affordable projects incrementally (rather than rescanning all projects every round) keeps the total unlocking work to O(n log n) across the entire process.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n + k log n), for the sort plus up to k heap operations.
Space: O(n) for the heap and sorted list.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

IPO is a strong example of the "greedy with two heaps" pattern: one structure (sorted list or min-heap) to determine ELIGIBILITY, another (max-heap) to determine the BEST choice among eligible options at each step.
Common Mistakes

items: Rescanning all projects for affordability every round instead of using a sorted pointer sweep, degrading efficiency.
Forgetting to stop early once the max-heap is empty (no affordable projects remain), potentially trying to process more rounds than possible.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["No project is ever affordable given the starting capital","The final capital equals the starting capital w, since no projects can be taken."],["k exceeds the number of profitable opportunities available","The loop simply stops early once the max-heap becomes empty."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly stating the exchange argument ("since capital never decreases, taking the best AFFORDABLE option now is never worse than saving it for later") justifies the greedy approach rigorously, not just by intuition.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "repeatedly pick the best available option as eligibility grows over time", think: two-heap greedy, one for eligibility, one for best-choice selection.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you also report WHICH projects were chosen, not just the final capital?
How would this change if projects could be taken multiple times?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "greedy with two heaps: one for eligibility, one for best-choice" problem, a broadly reusable technique.
Task Scheduler and similar problems using a max-heap to always pick the currently-best option.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Recursive sequence exploration costs O(n^k) time, utterly infeasible at scale; the two-heap greedy approach costs O(n log n + k log n) time and O(n) space, the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: greedy with two heaps: a sorted list (or min-heap) for eligibility by capital requirement, a max-heap for choosing the best profit among eligible projects.
Core Idea: each round, unlock all newly affordable projects into the max-heap, then take the highest-profit one, adding it to capital.
Time: O(n^k) for recursive exploration, O(n log n + k log n) for the optimized two-heap greedy.
Space: O(k) recursion depth versus O(n) for the heap.
Most Important Observation: since capital never decreases, taking the best affordable project now is always at least as good as any alternative strategy.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, moderately hard greedy problem combining sorting with a max-heap.
One line memory trick: sort by capital needed; unlock and pick the highest-profit affordable project, k times.
